was platted in the early 20th century as a regular grid of numbered streets and avenues, but that grid was never drawn on a blank slate. Street right-of-way widths across Jackson Heights range enormously, and that range mirrors the split between quiet residential blocks built for courtyard gardens and wider diagonal roads built to carry commerce and transit.","cites":["nyc-opendata","nyc-parks"],"claim_ids":["c-mean-width","c-min-width","c-max-width"],"slides":[{"title":"An Average Width, a Wide Range","body":"Street segments in Jackson Heights average about 32.6 feet wide — but that average hides a striking range, from narrow six-foot mews and service lanes tucked between garden apartment buildings to seventy-foot boulevards built to carry traffic and trolleys.","map":{"item_id":"81186482d5dd48ca9882593adadd6bfe","caption":"Range of street widths across the neighbourhood."},"claim_ids":["c-mean-width"]},{"title":"From Six Feet to Seventy",
"body":"The narrowest recorded segment, just 6 feet wide, is the kind of private garden path or service alley that lets light and air reach interior courtyards. The widest, at 70 feet, belongs to the diagonal boulevards — a nearly twelvefold difference that captures, in one statistic, how street and open space systems were built to complement each other.","map":{"item_id":"865dbb45a3b3455590652560174b9ed9","caption":"Narrowest and widest street segments compared."},"claim_ids":["c-min-width","c-max-width"]}]}]}
